newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh says tax evasion hurts economy.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh says tax evasion hurts economy.

text.p: Bangladesh Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria said on Tuesday widespread tax evasion was hurting the country's economy, still heavily dependent on foreign assistance.

"The tendency of evading duties and taxes is primarily responsible for the poor performace of revenue collection. And this blocks development efforts of the government," he told a meeting of revenue officials and entrepreneurs on proposals for the budget for fiscal 1997/98, beginning next July.
Kibria said the government policy of gradually reducing taxes and duties was not showing any positive effect on revenue.
"The situation is not improving even after extensive reduction of the rates of income tax and import duties," he said.
The finance minister said only 638,000 people paid income tax in a country of 120 million people.
"The existing tax exemption, particularly in import duties, is responsible for the shrinking of the base of the country's tax system," he said.
The present exemption for individual annual income taxpayers is 60,000 taka ($1,370) and manufacturing industries, tourism and organisations providing infrastructure get tax breaks.
Import duties range between 2.5 percent and 45 percent. The government has exempted duty on imports of capital machinery for export-oriented companies.
Bangladesh also levies Value Added Tax (VAT) at a rate of 15 percent. The country has set target revenues at 130.4 billion taka ($3.0 billion) for fiscal 1996/97.
The country's fiscal deficit was 6.2 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1995/96.
"Bangladesh has so far failed to build up an ideal tax system due to the provision of tax exemption and other incentives," Kibria said.

He said said it was imperative Bangladesh mobilise more internal resources. "The hope for availability of foreign aid is gradually shrinking. Moreover, the aid with stringent conditions is not acceptable to us," he said without elaborating.
The finance minister said there was pressure on the government from donors to finance infratructure development and alleviate poverty from the country's own resources.
Bangladesh receives about $1.7 billion in foreign assistance to finance its annual development and imports.
Nearly 50 percent of Bangladesh's population live below the poverty line. The country's annual per capita income is $240.
